item.subskill: Find the whole from a part and its percent
item.grade_rationale: Mid for grade 6: 6.RP.3c finding the whole given a part and the percent. One step that needs the grade's key idea (27 is 15 hundredths of the whole, so divide by 0.15 or scale 15% to 100%). About half of grade 6 sets it up as a division; the rest multiply or stop the scaling early.
item.prompt: Mia has saved $27 for a new bike. The amount she has saved is 15% of the price of the bike. What is the price of the bike, in dollars?
item.explanation: 15% of the price is $27. Then 5% of the price is 27 / 3 = 9 dollars, and 100% is 20 x 9 = 180 dollars. (Or: 27 / 0.15 = 180.) Check: 15% of 180 is 0.15 x 180 = 27.
mechanism: scale the percent to 100% (divide by the decimal)
item.quantity_asked: the price of the bike in dollars, given that $27 is 15% of it

plugback.why: A student can take 15% of an option and compare it with $27 in one multiplication; the key is the third option in ascending order.

90.misconception: treats the 5% value as 10% when scaling to 100%
90.why: The student finds 5% = 27 / 3 = 9 but then multiplies by 10, as if 9 were 10% of the price, getting 90.

162.misconception: scales 15% only to 90% (drops the remainder of 100 / 15)
162.why: The student sees that 15% fits into 100% about 6 times (15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90) and multiplies 27 by 6, stopping at 90% of the price.

405.misconception: reads 15% as one fifteenth and multiplies by 15
405.why: The student thinks $27 is one fifteenth of the price and multiplies 27 x 15 = 405 instead of dividing by 0.15.

item.structure_check: Interior key: two options below (90, 162) and one above (405); the stem does not say which side an error falls on.
item.intermediate_check: 90: no, it is not a step of either correct path (5% = 9 and 10% = 18 are the steps; 90 is 50%). 162: no, 90% of the price is not computed in the solution. 405: no, 27 x 15 is not a step. None follows from the key through one printed rate.
item.shape_check: The stem hands over: the price is more than $27 (all four), 15% is less than one quarter so the price is more than 4 x 27 = 108 (strikes 90), 15% is more than one tenth so the price is less than 10 x 27 = 270 (strikes 405). 162 and 180 survive together.
item.interior_parity_check: Middle values 162 and 180: both three-digit whole numbers of dollars; the key is not the only round number in the set (90 is round too).
item.arith_class_check: Whole dollars all four. The key is not alone as a multiple of 10 (90 is one), not alone as even (90, 162 are even), not a perfect square. Being a multiple of 20 (forced by 15% = 3/20 of a whole-dollar price) is only readable after setting up the division, which is the solution.

item.subskill: Unit price from a pack, then the cost of a larger count
item.grade_rationale: Low for grade 6: 6.RP.3b unit pricing in two routine steps (divide the pack price by 6, multiply by 9). The only care point is that 9 is not a whole number of packs; most grade 6 students find the unit price and multiply.
item.prompt: A bakery sells muffins in packs of 6 for $7.44. Sam wants 9 muffins, and the bakery will sell them to him at the same price for each muffin. How many dollars will Sam pay for 9 muffins?
item.explanation: First find the price of one muffin: 7.44 / 6 = 1.24 dollars. Then multiply by the number of muffins: 9 x 1.24 = 11.16. Sam pays $11.16.
mechanism: price of one item from a pack price
multiply the unit price by a count that is not a whole number of packs
item.quantity_asked: the cost, in dollars, of 9 muffins at the pack's price per muffin

plugback.why: An option can only be checked by finding the unit price (7.44 / 6) and comparing it with the option divided by 9: that is the whole solution, not a shortcut.

9.92.misconception: finds the cost of the 3 extra muffins by dividing the pack price by 3
9.92.why: The student sees 3 more muffins and divides $7.44 by 3 to price them (2.48) instead of by 2 for half a pack, giving 7.44 + 2.48 = 9.92.

10.50.misconception: drops the cents and works with a $7 pack price
10.50.why: The student uses $7 instead of $7.44 because the cents look small, so one muffin costs 7 / 6 and 9 muffins cost 1.5 x 7 = 10.50.

14.88.misconception: rounds up to whole packs although muffins are priced singly
14.88.why: The student thinks 9 muffins need 2 packs and pays 2 x 7.44 = 14.88, ignoring that the stem sells each muffin at the same price.

item.structure_check: Interior key; the stem gives no direction to the errors (one below from a wrong share of the pack, one below from dropping the cents, one above from whole packs).
item.intermediate_check: 9.92: no, it is 8 muffins cost, which no correct path computes. 10.50: no, it uses a $7 pack price that never appears in the solution. 14.88: no, two whole packs are never computed in the correct path (the solution uses one muffin price 1.24, which is not an option).
item.shape_check: The stem hands over: more than one pack (so more than 7.44: all four survive), fewer than two packs (under 14.88: strikes 14.88 only), dollars and cents (all survive). Three options survive every property together.
item.interior_parity_check: Middle values 10.50 and 11.16: both dollars with two decimal places; the key is not the cleaner one (10.50 is cleaner).
item.arith_class_check: No forced class: the key is 9 x 1.24, and nothing printed forces a digit or a multiple a student could test without finding the unit price. All four options are in cents with two decimals.

item.subskill: One expression for two kinds of boxes shared equally
item.grade_rationale: Mid for grade 5: the story is one expression, (6 x 21 + 8 x 6) / 3 (5.OA.A.2), with two products, a sum and a quotient. The key idea is that the whole total is shared, so both products sit inside the grouping. About half of grade-5 students write and evaluate it correctly; the rest share only part, mix up which count goes with which box, or use one box size for every box.
item.prompt: A coach buys 6 boxes with 21 tennis balls in each box and 8 boxes with 6 tennis balls in each box. She shares all the tennis balls equally among 3 teams. How many tennis balls does each team get?
item.explanation: The large boxes hold 6 x 21 = 126 balls and the small boxes hold 8 x 6 = 48 balls, so there are 126 + 48 = 174 balls. Shared among 3 teams: 174 / 3 = 58. As one expression: (6 x 21 + 8 x 6) / 3 = 58.
mechanism: two products for two kinds of boxes
divide the whole total by the number of teams
item.quantity_asked: the number of tennis balls each team gets

plugback.why: An option is the result of the story, not a starting value; checking it means rebuilding the total 174 and dividing, which is solving. The key sits at ascending try 2 for that reason.

28.misconception: uses one box size for every box
28.why: Adds the boxes, 6 + 8 = 14, and uses 6 balls for each: 14 x 6 = 84, and 84 / 3 = 28.

68.misconception: pairs each number of boxes with the wrong box size
68.why: Uses 6 boxes of 6 and 8 boxes of 21: 36 + 168 = 204, and 204 / 3 = 68.

90.misconception: writes the expression without grouping, so only the first product is shared
90.why: Writes 6 x 21 / 3 + 8 x 6: 126 / 3 = 42, then adds all 48 small-box balls: 42 + 48 = 90.

item.structure_check: Interior key: using the small size for every box (28) falls below; swapping the pairs (68) and sharing only the first product (90) fall above.
item.intermediate_check: 68: no, 204 / 3 uses a total the chain never forms. 90: no, 42 + 48 mixes a shared part with an unshared part; it is not the key moved by one printed number (90 - 58 = 32 is not printed or a sum of two printed numbers). 28: no, 84 / 3; 58 - 28 = 30 is not printed. The intermediates 126, 48 and 174 are not options.
item.shape_check: Whole number (all four). Each team gets at least the large boxes' share, 126 / 3 = 42 (strikes 28 only). If every box held 21, each team would get 14 x 21 / 3 = 98, so fewer than 98 (strikes none). 58, 68 and 90 survive together.
item.interior_parity_check: The two middle values are 58 and 68: both two-digit even numbers ending in 8; same form, the key is not cleaner.
item.arith_class_check: No class is forced (174 / 3 has no stem-readable parity or final digit before computing). All options are even; 28, 58 and 68 end in 8, so the key is not alone.
